pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** What Plants Need to Grow

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y2 'Plants'):** 'find out and describe how plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy' — the three factors are named explicitly, and the verb 'find out' signals a first-hand comparative investigation rather than being told.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-LS2-1):** '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1]' [Assessment Boundary: testing one variable at a time]; DCI LS2.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1].' Honest note: NGSS names water + sunlight but NOT temperature — 'suitable temperature' is the UK-specific third factor.

- **Operational details:** The concept is causal and best FELT through a controlled comparison: identical plants, change ONE thing (no light / no water / cold), keep the rest the same, watch what happens over days. The learning is the CONTRAST — the deprived plant beside the healthy one — not a list recited. Because real plants take a week+ to respond, first-hand growing (cress on a windowsill, one pot in a cupboard) is the gold standard and should anchor the topic; a simulation earns its place by COMPRESSING that week into seconds so the child can run many what-ifs and isolate each factor. Emphasise the fair-test move implicitly: change one thing at a time (the NGSS assessment boundary) so the child can attribute the effect to that factor. Keep it to the three named factors at this age — do NOT introduce photosynthesis or soil-as-food (KS2/KS3).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child predicts what will happen to a plant kept in the dark / unwatered / frozen, runs or observes the comparison, and describes the result — 'the one in the cupboard went pale and floppy because it had no light' — attributing the change to the single factor that was removed.
bestPractices: Anchor in a real, first-hand growing comparison (cress/bean on the windowsill vs in a dark cupboard; watered vs unwatered) — plants changing over days is the evidence; nothing substitutes for having grown one.
Change ONE factor at a time and keep the others the same (the NGSS fair-test boundary) so the effect can be pinned to that factor — model this explicitly with paired pots.
Use predict–observe–explain: have the child commit to a prediction BEFORE seeing the outcome, so the surprising result (pale, leggy, wilted) does the teaching.
Keep to the three named factors (water, light, suitable temperature); resist 'plants eat soil/food' framing — that misconception is tackled properly later (KS2 Y3+).
Give the healthy control equal prominence — the concept lives in the CONTRAST between deprived and thriving plants, so always show them side by side.
keyRepresentations: Paired-pot comparison: identical plants side by side, one deprived of a single factor — the canonical fair-test image.
A time strip / growth diary: same plant drawn day 1, 3, 5, 7 to make slow change visible.
A simple 'plant needs' icon set (watering can, sun, thermometer) used as labels on each condition.
A cause→effect pairing (dark → pale & leggy; no water → wilted & dry; cold → stunted) shown as before/after.
commonMisconceptions: 'Plants get their food from the soil' — the dominant and durable error; at this age keep to water/light/warmth and avoid feeding language, but do not reinforce soil-as-food.
'Plants don't really need light, they just need water' — children over-weight watering (visible care) and under-weight light; the dark-cupboard result is the essential counter.
Thinking a plant in the dark that is still green/standing is 'fine' — needs longer observation to see it go pale and leggy (etiolation).
Believing plants need exactly the same conditions as animals (e.g. must be warm/indoors), missing that 'suitable' varies by plant.
Assuming more of a good thing is always better (drowning a plant with water, scorching heat) rather than 'suitable' amounts.

learn.summary: For ages 6–8, teach that plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy by running controlled, one-factor-at-a-time comparisons: a plant deprived of a single need placed beside a thriving control. The concept lives in the CONTRAST over time, with predict-before-observe locking in a guess so a surprising result (pale, leggy, wilted) does the teaching. Anchor in a real first-hand growing comparison; a fast-forward simulation earns its place by compressing a week into seconds so children can run many what-ifs. Keep to the three named factors and avoid soil-as-food framing (addressed later at KS2).

activities.title: Windowsill vs cupboard: a real cress comparison
feedback: If the child predicts both plants will look the same because both are watered, point to the pale, floppy dark plant: 'The cupboard plant got water too — so why isn't it healthy? What did it miss out on?'

If the child says the plant just needs feeding, explain that plants are not fed like pets or people; the needs we are testing are light, water and a suitable temperature, so watering is not the same as feeding — save exactly how plants use these for later (KS2).
Reinforce: 'The one in the cupboard went pale and floppy because it had no light' — attribute the change to the single factor that was removed.
If the dark plant still looks green and standing after a day or two, keep observing: etiolation takes time, so don't judge it 'fine' early.
activities.rationale: The UK Y2 verb 'find out' and NGSS 'plan and conduct an investigation' both signal first-hand comparative work rather than being told. Real plants changing over days are the evidence, and predict-observe-explain makes the surprising result the teacher. Keeping both pots similarly moist (check the soil, because a sunny windowsill dries pots faster) takes water out of the comparison, so light is the main difference. A sunny windowsill may also be warmer, so this is a simple comparison the child can read rather than a perfectly controlled test.
sourceClaims: DfE Y2 statutory: 'find out and describe how plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy'.

NGSS 2-LS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1]' with assessment boundary 'testing one variable at a time'; DCI LS2.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1].' NGSS names water+sunlight, not temperature.
learnerActions: Start with two identical pots of young green cress (or bean) seedlings, keep both soils similarly moist, and put one on a bright windowsill and one in a dark cupboard.
Before waiting, write or say a prediction: how will each plant look after a week, and WHY?
Keep a growth diary: draw the same plant on day 1, 3, 5 and 7 to make the slow change visible.
After a week, describe the result and name which single need was missing for the cupboard plant.
activities.intendedInsight: Light is a genuine growth need, not an optional extra — watering alone does not keep a plant healthy. Over days the dark plant goes pale, leggy and floppy while its watered twin in the light stays green and sturdy.

activities.title: Grow-lab: one dial at a time
feedback: If two factors are changed at once, prompt: 'Change just one thing so you know what caused it.'

Draw attention to the key moment: watching the test plant change (the dark plant stretching tall and pale, the dry plant wilting, the cold plant growing slowly) while its twin stays green and healthy shows which need was missing — and fast enough to test another.

Connect back to the real pots: 'Did the sim show the same thing your cupboard cress did? If it did, that helps us trust it about light — we would need real plants to check the water and temperature results too.'
activities.rationale: The content is causal and time-based, so compressing a week into seconds lets a child run many repeatable, one-variable trials that a single slow pot cannot. A guardrail that blocks changing two dials at once quietly teaches the NGSS fair-test boundary. A time-lapse model is one way to make slow change visible; it is a scaffold layered on first-hand growing, not a substitute for it, so the simulation should be confirmed against the real investigation.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-LS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1]' with assessment boundary 'testing one variable at a time'; DCI LS2.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1].' NGSS names water+sunlight, not temperature.
learnerActions: Use a fast-forward grow-lab (or an adult-run paper/role-play version) with two identical seedlings: a 'test' plant you can change and a 'control' you keep fixed.
Change ONLY ONE thing on the test plant — turn its light off (or bright/dim), give it no water or lots of water, or make it cold/warm/hot — and leave everything else the same as the control.
Lock in a prediction, then start the grow so days tick past in seconds and watch how the test plant responds.
Run it again with a different single dial (water, then temperature) and compare each result to the healthy control.
activities.intendedInsight: When you change one factor and keep the rest the same, you can pin the effect to that factor. Each missing need produces a recognisable result: dark → pale and leggy; no water → wilted and dry; cold → stunted growth.

activities.title: Match the cause to the effect (recap/reference)
feedback: If the child only names water as important, revisit the dark-plant result: being watered did not keep it healthy.
If 'food' or 'soil-as-food' appears, redirect to water, light and warmth without reinforcing feeding language.
Prompt that drowning a plant or scorching heat harms it too — 'suitable' is a sweet spot, not 'as much as possible'.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or matching recap names each factor and its effect and is useful for consolidation and reference. On its own it shows the conclusion rather than generating it, so it supports but does not replace running the comparison. Giving the healthy control equal prominence keeps the concept in the contrast.
learnerActions: Study a before/after set pairing each deprivation with its symptom: dark → pale and leggy; no water → wilted and dry; cold → stunted.
Tap or point to a pale cupboard-plant, a wilted dry plant, and a healthy control and say which need each one had or lacked.
Match condition icons (watering can, sun, thermometer) to the plant outcomes.
Use a 'how much water is suitable?' choice to show that more is not always better — too much drowns, too little dries.
activities.intendedInsight: Each of the three named needs has a distinct effect when missing, and 'suitable' means a right amount — not maximum. The healthy control shows what all three together look like.

constraints: Keep to the three named factors at this age — water, light and suitable temperature. Do NOT introduce photosynthesis or soil-as-food; that misconception is tackled properly later (KS2 Y3+).

Do not reinforce 'plants eat soil/food' framing; counter animal-style feeding only by noting plants are not fed like animals and that the needs we are studying are light, water and a suitable temperature — do not explain the food-making mechanism at this age.

A static poster or matching/recap task shows the conclusion and is suitable as consolidation or reference, not as the sole route to building the causal understanding — pair it with an actual comparison.
A multiple-choice or matching check tests prediction and cause-to-effect recognition after the fact; recognition alone does not elicit the first-hand observation that builds the causal idea.
A time-lapse simulation is a scaffold that compresses time; it should be anchored to a real first-hand growing comparison so children confirm the sim matches reality.
'Suitable' temperature varies by plant — do not imply plants need exactly the same warm/indoor conditions as animals, and do not treat 'more is always better'.

Real plants can take several days to a week or more to show clear changes (lack of water may show sooner); plan for longer observation so a still-green dark plant is seen to go pale and leggy (etiolation) rather than judged 'fine' early.
If a real cold condition is attempted, supervise it and treat outcomes as variable; a simulated or described cold test is often safer than relying on a specific absolute 'frozen' result.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
NGSS 2-LS2-1 names water and sunlight but NOT temperature; 'suitable temperature' is the UK Y2 (DfE) third factor. Keep this distinction when citing standards.
The OU OpenLearn source on the soil-as-food misconception is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its claim as unconfirmed and do not rest any activity on it as evidence.

The original 'conversation' and '3D' catalog entries asserted these formats 'add nothing' or would be a 'gimmick'. Those are fit opinions, not established limits, so they were not carried as universal claims; a flat side-by-side comparison is sufficient for this content, but that does not prove other media cannot teach it.

Cold/freezing as a demonstration: a home freezer can kill a plant and outcomes depend on plant and setup; describe or simulate the cold condition rather than relying on a specific absolute 'frozen' result, and supervise any real cold test.
The anti-feeding counter is kept minimal and deliberately does not name or explain photosynthesis, per the age-stage constraint; whether to use the word 'food' at all is a teacher judgement.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: set up two identical watered cress pots, one in light and one in a dark cupboard. Ask the child to predict how each looks after a week and WHY, before waiting. A 'water is enough' model predicts both healthy. The dark plant grows pale and spindly. The pre-observation reasoning about light as a need is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: The cupboard plant got water — so why didn't the water keep it healthy?
What three things does a plant need to grow well?
If I put a healthy plant in the freezer but kept watering it, what would happen? Which need is missing?
How is 'giving a plant water' different from 'feeding' an animal?
assess.correctAnswer: Different: the windowsill plant grows healthy and green; the cupboard plant grows pale, spindly and weak (or dies) because it has NO LIGHT. Plants need light (as well as water and a suitable temperature) to grow and stay healthy — water alone is not enough. Full marks name light as the missing need and predict the unhealthy outcome.

errorPatterns.pattern: as long as it has water (and soil) a plant is fine — light doesn't really matter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run the windowsill-vs-cupboard test; the pale, floppy dark plant shows light IS a need, not an extra.
errorPatterns.distractor: They'll look the same, because both plants are being watered.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts both plants look the same because both are watered

errorPatterns.pattern: plants need to be given food to grow (animal-like feeding)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plants aren't fed like pets — with light + water + warmth they make their own food. Distinguish giving water from giving food.
errorPatterns.distractor: The cupboard plant will be fine if I remember to feed it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: lists 'food' among what you must give the plant

errorPatterns.pattern: plants don't need warmth / any temperature is fine
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recall that a frosted or frozen plant wilts/dies — a suitable temperature is one of the needs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: omits suitable temperature; thinks a freezing plant grows normally

responseLevels.gap: Predicts both plants the same because both watered; thinks water/soil alone suffices or plants must be fed.
responseLevels.full: Predicts the dark plant grows pale/weak because light is missing, names all three needs (water, light, suitable temperature), and explains a plant makes its own food rather than being fed — transferring to a freezing-plant case.
responseLevels.partial: Names light as needed and predicts a difference, but can't fully separate the three needs or still slips 'food' into the list — the need recognised without the full set.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I have two identical little cress plants. One I keep on a sunny windowsill and water it; the other I put in a dark cupboard but still water it. After a week, will they look the same or different — and the important part, WHY? What does the cupboard one miss out on?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who knows light is a genuine growth NEED from one who thinks water (or soil) alone keeps a plant healthy. Watering both removes water as the variable, so only a child who values light predicts the dark plant will suffer.
